notes.1: This measuring question was generally answered correctly. The most common incorrect answer was 7.9.
notes.2: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.3: This question was generally well answered. There were some answers of 50%, presumably from $72.50 ÷ $1.45 = 50. The other common error was 1.45 × 72.5 ÷ 100 = 1.05.
notes.4: This question was well answered by the majority of candidates. The most common error was to give the answer 6.6 rather than an answer to 3 significant figures. The answer should be fully evaluated rather than given as a fraction.
notes.5: Many candidates knew they had to put a bracket into their answer and several were able to gain the mark. Others were unsure of how to deal with the first y and took it as the factor but then just wrote 2y or –2y inside the bracket.
notes.6: This question was very well answered with the vast majority clearly understanding the rules for subtracting vectors. Most errors were due to a lack of understanding of directed numbers. For the first component, the common error was −1 from 2 − 3 rather than 2 − (−3). Only a few candidates wrote a fraction line.      
notes.7: Many candidates knew to draw a vertical and horizontal line and scored both marks. A significant number also added diagonals.
notes.8: Many candidates showed a good understanding of dividing in a given ratio. The most common error was to divide 72 by 5 and then by 4, giving answers of 14.4 and 18. Some gave amounts not adding to 72.
notes.10: Whilst many candidates were able to give the correct simplification, there were a significant number who did not understand which sign applies to which term. A small number tried to factorise and gave their answer as p(2 – 5) – q(1 – 3) or similar.
notes.12: Many candidates had followed the wording of the question and scored both marks. Candidates needed to show clear, full working.
notes.14: Almost all candidates understood the term factor. Very few listed any numbers which weren’t factors of 30. The most common reason for not scoring both marks was due to not listing all the factors; usually 1 and 30 were omitted.
notes.15: The majority of candidates scored both marks.
notes.17: Many candidates appeared not to understand what was required for this question. Some scored one mark for 30.5 with 31.4 or otherwise as the 2nd value. Several gave integer answers, commonly 30 and 32.
notes.20: Many candidates were unable to give the correct answer. Several scored one mark for 360 ÷ 20. Many did not show any method.
notes.21: The majority of candidates scored full marks. The common errors were 95 ÷ 10, 2.43 from the error 0 × 5 = 5 and 2 from 10 ÷ 5, not from rounding the correct answer.
notes.22: The majority of candidates were able to give the correct answer. Of those who did not, the majority were unable to use ratio and gave the answer 11, subtracting 12 from 23.
notes.24: The majority of candidates made an attempt at this question and some scored full marks. Several scored one mark and others wrote various conversions, e.g. 108 km = 108 000 m or 1 min = 60 seconds but did not know what to do after that.
notes.25: Quite a few correct answers were seen in this question, almost all from using the formula. Several gave the interest instead of the value of the investment. A small number of candidates calculated simple interest.
notes.key_messages: Ensure answers are given to the required accuracy and avoid premature rounding in working. When a question states without a calculator and that you must show all your working, credit will not be given to candidates who use a calculator and do not show full working. Care needs to be taken with writing, particularly figures which are often not clear.
notes.general_comments: The standard of candidates’ responses was generally very good. The majority of candidates appeared to have had sufficient time to complete the paper. Rounding to 3 significant figures is stated in the rubric. Non-exact answers to less than 3 figures will lose at least accuracy marks unless a more accurate answer is seen in the working. This was seen quite often in Questions 4 and 21 where 6.6 and 2.4 were given as answers, without more accurate values being shown in the method. Revision should include basic skills as well as the advanced topics; many candidates could not handle basic place value in Question 13(a).
notes.9a: Most candidates gave the correct answer. There were a small number who gave the answer 13.
notes.9b: This part was also very well answered. The main error was 12 from 15 – 3.
notes.11a: Some candidates gave the correct answer. There appeared to be a lack of understanding of significant figures and many appeared to confuse the term significant figures and decimal places. 0.08 was a common incorrect answer.
notes.11b: This part was less well answered with many not writing place holders, leading to 10 as a common incorrect answer; the other common incorrect answer was 10100.
notes.13a: This part was generally well answered. The most common errors were as a result of not understanding place value, as shown by answers of 5200007, 500200007, 5207000.
notes.13b: This part was less well answered. Many made an attempt at using a power of 10 but it wasn’t –4 written in standard form, e.g. 81.3 × 10 . –3
notes.16a: Many candidates clearly understood the term gradient but gave the answer as 4x rather than 4.
notes.16b: This part was less well answered. A common error was to give the answer 6 rather than –6. Several candidates did not attempt to answer this part.
notes.18a: Many candidates were able to give the correct answer. Some clearly knew the median as the middle value but had not listed the values in order first, and gave the answer as 46.5 from 73 and 20, the middle values in the original list. Some correctly ordered the list but were unable to work out the mean of 20 and 23, giving the answer 22. A small number calculated the mean rather than the median.
notes.18b: This part was less well answered. A common error again was not thinking about the order of the numbers and just calculating 54 – 16. Some who had correctly used the highest and lowest values wrote 95 – 7 on the answer line without resolving it.
notes.19a: Most candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.19b: Many were able to give the correct answer and showed method. The most common error was to use 48 as one of the base angles and give the answer as 84.
notes.23a: Many candidates gave the correct answer. A small number reversed the co-ordinates.
notes.23b: This part was also well answered. Those who had reversed the co-ordinates in part (a) generally did so in this part also.
notes.23c: This part was less well answered than the previous parts. There were various combinations of ±2 and ±8. −8      
notes.26a: Many candidates were able to give the correct answer. A small number subtracted 7 rather than added. A small number ‘simplified’ 3w – 7 to –4w.
notes.26b: Again many correct answers were seen in this part. Some made numerical slips when multiplying out the bracket. Some who gave the answer as a fraction had not cancelled to its simplest form.
